newsitem.title: USA: IRS offers Fla. tax filers Disney World option.
newsitem.headline: IRS offers Fla. tax filers Disney World option.

text.p: - In an effort to put a more human face on the daunting and formidable Internal Revenue Service, IRS advisers descended on Walt Disney World Tuesday, offering last minute tax guidance to beleaguered procrastinators.
And despite a light rain dozens of filers showed up, often standing in lines as long as those for the nearby Comedy Warehouse.
"This is great," said Edward Sanderson, who brought a box full of receipts and tax forms with him. "I had an appointment with H&R Block, but then I heard about this. I'm saving a hundred bucks."
Well, almost. There was a $19 charge to get inside Disney's Pleasure Island, a six-acre nightclub complex on Lake Buena Vista where the IRS set up temporary office.

But the IRS agents were able to explain to Sanderson why his wife's tax bill went up even though her income did not. And if the answer did not exactly make the young couple happy, they did say it gave them peace of mind hearing it from the IRS itself.
"I can't believe I went on vacation and forgot about taxes," said a chagrined Bill Summers of Dearpoint, Mich.

"Here I was in a strange city and I thought I'd spend the whole day trying to find a post office that still had some extension forms. Then I heard about this and took the kids to Planet Hollywood instead."

Susan Carroll, the marketing expert who helped bring the IRS to Disney, was beaming as The Beatles song "Taxman" blared from loudspeakers throughout the park. "I'd say its been a great success," she said.
"We wanted to give people some extra tax help -- but yes, it's also a way to put a more human face on the IRS."

The IRS advisers came on duty at 6 p.m. EDT, their laptop computers fully charged for optional electronic filing. They stayed until midnight, the cutoff time for postal workers accompanying them to accept returns.
The IRS estimates it will collect about $1.5 trillion from U.S. taxpayers this year. Most are not likely to recall it as a warm, fuzzy experience.
So, did filing at Disney World make Sheila Margolis of Cassleberry, Florida, happier that the government was getting almost $6,000 from her this year?
"Well, when you put it like that, maybe not," she said. "But anything that makes tax day a little better is okay with me. Last year, I just drove to the post office. Now, Im going to go dancing."
